result:
Short version: Apache's EBCDIC tables aren't the stock IBM ones — they've been tweaked precisely around the newline, because on z/OS the C `'\n'` is EBCDIC **0x15 (NL)**, not 0x25 (LF). To make `'\n'` come out as ASCII LF on the wire, httpd swaps the newline pair.

**ASCII 0x0A → which EBCDIC byte?**
`0x15` (NL). The `os_toebcdic` table maps `0x0A → 0x15`.

**Does it come back?**
Yes. `os_toascii[0x15] = 0x0A`, so `0x0A → 0x15 → 0x0A` round-trips cleanly. Apache keeps the two tables as exact inverses of one another (they have to, since binary data also passes through this layer), so every byte round-trips.

**EBCDIC 0x25 arriving from elsewhere?**
This is the trap. Because the newline pair is swapped, `0x25` is no longer "the LF byte" as far as httpd is concerned. `os_toascii[0x25] = 0x85` — i.e. it turns into the C1 control **NEL (0x85)**, *not* ASCII 0x0A. It will round-trip fine (`0x25 → 0x85 → 0x25`), but if you were expecting a stray 0x25 to show up as an ASCII newline, it won't. Only 0x15 does that now.

So the mapping around the newline is effectively:

| direction | byte | result |
|---|---|---|
| to ASCII | EBCDIC 0x15 | ASCII 0x0A |
| to ASCII | EBCDIC 0x25 | ASCII 0x85 (NEL) |
| to EBCDIC | ASCII 0x0A | EBCDIC 0x15 |
| to EBCDIC | ASCII 0x85 | EBCDIC 0x25 |

Practical upshot: if the "somewhere else" is another EBCDIC system (or a dataset) that uses 0x25 as its line terminator, those lines will *not* be seen as newlines after passing through httpd's layer — you'd want to normalize 0x25 → 0x15 before it enters the conversion, or the line breaks will silently turn into NEL characters on the ASCII side.
